name: Sideburns

card.summary: Hair left to grow in front of the ears, which men shape in length and width to frame the face, change how long or wide it looks, and cover or sharpen the jawline and temples.
card.aka: sideboards; side whiskers; burnsides; mutton chops (long form)
card.note: Looksmax.org posters debate how sideburn shape suits different face shapes; recession at the temples and sideburns can be a sign of frontal fibrosing alopecia.

quick.overview:
Sideburns are the strips of facial hair that run down in front of the ears. Because they sit at the edge of the face, their length, width and shape change how the temples, cheekbones and jaw read, and men use them as a styling tool in the same way they use a hairstyle or a beard.

Barbers usually shape them with clippers and a razor line. In looksmaxxing forums the discussion is about "optimal" length and where the bottom line should end relative to the jaw, and some posters argue that sideburn choices should follow face structure. Published research on the style question is absent; the medical literature touches sideburns mainly in surgery and hair-loss papers.
quick.how: In practice sideburns are grown out, then trimmed to a chosen length and width, with the lower edge cleaned up with a trimmer or razor. They are often blended into a beard or fade into the haircut. Facial surgeons and hair-transplant surgeons also plan around them, and sideburn hair can be restored by grafting.
quick.risks: Trimming carries ordinary shaving risks such as irritation and ingrown hairs. Loss of hair in the sideburn and beard area, especially together with receding temples and eyebrow thinning, is described in dermatology literature as a feature of frontal fibrosing alopecia in men, which a dermatologist can assess.

lead: Sideburns, also called sideboards or side whiskers, are patches of facial hair grown on the sides of the face from the hairline to near or past the ears. The English word is a 19th-century alteration of "burnsides", after the American Civil War general Ambrose Burnside, who wore thick side hair joined to a moustache.[1] They are among the simplest ways a man can reshape the outline of his face without surgery, because the hair sits exactly where the temples, cheekbones and jaw meet the hairline.

Men use sideburns to frame the face. Length, width and the shape of the lower edge change how the temples and jaw look, and the hair can be left to blend into a beard, trimmed short with the hairline, or grown long as a stylistic statement. In looksmaxxing forums, threads on "optimal" sideburns compare lengths and shapes against face shape.[5]

Medical literature mentions sideburns mostly in a surgical context: facelift incisions for men are placed to keep the position and width of the sideburn natural,[2] and hair transplantation can restore sideburns along with the beard and eyebrows.[4] Dermatology reviews also note that early loss of sideburn and beard hair can be a sign of frontal fibrosing alopecia in men.[3]

angle.text: Sideburns change the outline of the face from the ear down toward the jaw. Men adjust their length and width to suit the haircut and beard, and some choose to blend or sharpen them to alter how long or wide the face looks.

paras: Sideburns run from the hairline toward or past the ears. Wikipedia lists several named forms: side whiskers (extravagant 19th-century growths hanging well below the jaw), mutton chops (the broad 19th-century style, often more extreme than modern sideburns), "friendly mutton chops" (sideburns joined to a moustache with a clean-shaven chin) and "lambchop" sideburns, which it associates with gay club scenes in San Francisco and Sydney.[1] If sideburns extend under the chin they become a beard, chinstrap or chin curtain.[1]
Short, tapered sideburns are common with modern haircuts and fades; long, wide ones are tied to retro and rock-and-roll looks.[1]

Side hair appears on Roman statues and masks from the first century, and Wikipedia notes the emperor Elagabalus is depicted with sideburns and a moustache.[1] In the nineteenth century young South American criollos copied the European fashion, and many independence-era portraits show leaders wearing them.[1] The engineer Werner von Siemens and the Finnish philosopher J. V. Snellman are also cited as wearers.[1]

Not every culture treated side hair the same way. Wikipedia describes "balcarrotas", long braided sideburns worn by Indigenous men in Colombia and Mexico, which colonial authorities in New Spain banned, a measure that led to rioting in 1692.[1]

Sideburns fell out of favour in the early twentieth century, and gas masks used in the First World War required a clean-shaven face for a seal; moustaches were unaffected.[1] Franklin Roosevelt briefly grew sideburns on a yachting cruise in 1936.[1]

They returned in the mid-1950s with Marlon Brando in The Wild One (1953) and Elvis Presley, becoming a signature of hoods, greasers and rockers.[1] They were worn by mods and hippies in the 1960s; a 1967 newspaper article covered a New Jersey youth's dispute over wearing them to his high school graduation.[1] By the 1970s they were common across all walks of life.[1]

Wikipedia associates sideburns with several images: Victorian formality, roughness or rebelliousness, rock and roll, and retro revival. Rock musicians including Stephen Stills, Neil Young, George Jones and Lemmy are named as having made them a signature look, and 21st-century wearers listed include Emmanuel Macron (short sideburns), Javier Milei, Cem Ozdemir, Viktor Yushchenko, Adam Sandler, John Lithgow and David Tennant.[1]

Looksmax.org has threads on choosing optimal sideburns and on whether sideburns suit particular ethnic backgrounds, with posters trading opinions about length, thickness and how the style interacts with jaw and hairline.[5][6] These are community opinions rather than tested guidance.

In one widely referenced guide thread, the author argues that sideburns are "extremely underrated" and that two common outcomes, bushy sideburns and a skin fade with none at all, are less flattering than full but short coverage ending mid-way down the ear; the poster says short side hair frames the lower third of the face and makes it look slimmer, whereas a skin fade can make the face look rounder.[5] Another thread argues the opposite for some men, saying sideburns make some faces read as less approachable and recommending a fade or sideburn taper instead.[6] Posters tie the choice to face and head shape, to the haircut and to how much beard is worn.[5][6]

Because sideburns sit at the edge of the face, surgeons plan around them. Hair transplant surgeons describe restoring sideburns together with eyebrows and beards as an established procedure.[4] Reports describe reconstructing a lost sideburn with a pre-expanded island scalp flap based on the superficial temporal vessels,[9] and modified cervicofacial flaps designed to keep a patient's sideburn shape and arrangement.[7] Incisions at the sideburn line are used for some jaw and cheek contouring operations, such as reduction malarplasty, and for lateral midface lifts.[11][12]

Surgeons describe a tailored approach to the male sideburn in facelifts, using temporal flap rotation and skin excision to keep its width and position and to hide scars in the hair and beard.[2] A review of facial hair restoration describes grafting of eyebrows, beards and sideburns as established procedures.[4] Case reports cover flap designs intended to preserve a patient's sideburns during facial surgery.[7]
Reviews of frontal fibrosing alopecia in men describe early involvement of the beard and sideburns, together with temporal recession and eyebrow loss.[3]

A trichoscopy study compared sideburn skin with frontotemporal scalp in frontal fibrosing alopecia and described features specific to the sideburn area, which is one reason dermatologists examine the sideburns when assessing hair loss at the temples.[10]

No studies found on how sideburn style affects perceived attractiveness. Surgical and dermatology papers (described above) cover sideburn hair restoration, incision placement and hair-loss conditions affecting the area.[2][3][4]

timeline.event: Side hair visible on Roman statues and masks.[1]
"Burnsides" becomes "sideburns" after General Ambrose Burnside; extravagant side whiskers and mutton chops are fashionable.[1]
Rioting follows the ban on long braided sideburns (balcarrotas) among Indigenous men in New Spain.[1]
First World War gas-mask seals require clean-shaven faces, accelerating the decline of sideburns.[1]
Marlon Brando wears sideburns in The Wild One.[1]
Elvis Presley's influence revives sideburns among rockers and greasers.[1]
Review describes sideburn restoration by hair transplantation as an established procedure.[4]
Review of frontal fibrosing alopecia in men describes early sideburn and beard involvement.[3]

lore.intro: Looksmax.org members discuss sideburns as a small framing tool, with threads on ideal length and on whether they suit particular ethnicities; some posters regard them as an underrated feature of the lower face, others recommend fades.[5][6]

claims.claim: There is an "optimal" sideburn length and shape: short, full coverage ending mid-way down the ear.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org guide says this shape frames the lower third of the face, slims it and defines the bones, compared with bushy sideburns or none.[5]
claims.experts: No published research has tested sideburn dimensions against attractiveness ratings.

claims.claim: Sideburns suit some ethnic groups less than others.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread argues that men of some backgrounds look better with a fade or taper than with sideburns.[6]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined this.

claims.claim: A skin fade with no sideburns makes the face look rounder.
claims.believers: The guide thread says hair carrying on into the sides of the head makes the face read rounder, while short sideburns accentuate the jaw area.[5]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested how sideburn presence changes perceived face width.

claims.claim: Long or bushy sideburns make the face look wider.
claims.believers: Posters describe unkempt, bushy sideburns as adding width and softness to the face.[5]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that nineteenth-century sideburns were far more extreme than modern ones and were fashionable in their time, so how they read depends on period and context.[1]

claims.claim: Receding sideburns can signal hair-loss conditions beyond ordinary balding.
claims.believers: Hair-loss discussions treat the temple and sideburn area as a place where thinning shows early.[3]
claims.experts: Reviews describe early loss of sideburn and beard hair, with temporal recession and eyebrow thinning, as a feature of frontal fibrosing alopecia in men, which dermatologists assess.[3][10]

claims.claim: Sideburns can be restored if lost.
claims.believers: Hair-restoration patients describe grafting to rebuild sideburns thinned by surgery, injury or hair loss.[4]
claims.experts: Surgical reviews and case reports describe sideburn transplantation and flap reconstruction as established options.[4][9]
